find-all-numbers-disappeared-in-an-array.pattern: Cyclic sort: value v belongs at index v − 1 (or mark index v − 1 as seen)

approaches.name: Scan for each number 1..n
approaches.idea: For every k from 1 to n, scan the whole array for k; if it is not there, k is missing.
steps: For `k` from 1 to n: scan `nums` for `k`.
If no element equals `k`, add `k` to the answer.
approaches.why: n candidates, each needing a full O(n) scan. With n = 10⁵ that is 10¹⁰ comparisons, far too slow.

approaches.name: Seen array
approaches.idea: Mark every value in a boolean array of size n + 1, then collect the unmarked numbers.
steps: Create `seen` of size n + 1 and set `seen[x] = true` for every `x` in `nums`.
Return every `k` from 1 to n with `seen[k]` false.
approaches.why: Two linear passes. The seen array is the O(n) extra space the follow-up asks you to avoid; it is still the right first answer to give in an interview.

approaches.name: Cyclic sort, then read the wrong slots
approaches.idea: Value v has a home at index v − 1. Swap every value into its home; afterwards, each index i that does not hold i + 1 is a number nobody came home to.
steps: Set `i = 0`. While `i < n`: let `home = nums[i] − 1`. If `nums[i] != nums[home]`, swap them (and stay at `i`); otherwise `i++`.
Scan: for every `i` with `nums[i] != i + 1`, add `i + 1` to the answer.
approaches.why: Each swap puts one value in its home for good, so there are at most n − 1 swaps plus n increments. Comparing `nums[i]` with `nums[home]` (not with `i + 1`) is what stops an endless loop when the home already holds a duplicate. In Python, compute `home` first: `nums[i], nums[nums[i] - 1] = …` assigns `nums[i]` before evaluating the second index.

approaches.name: Sign marking
approaches.idea: Use the sign of nums[v − 1] as the "seen" flag for v: make it negative. Numbers whose slot stays positive were never seen.
steps: For each value `v` (use `|v|`, it may already be negated): if `nums[|v| − 1] > 0`, negate it.
Every index `i` whose value is still positive means `i + 1` is missing.
approaches.why: Two passes and no extra memory. Unlike cyclic sort, nothing moves, so flipping the signs back afterwards restores the input exactly. It relies on every value being at least 1.

set-mismatch.pattern: Cyclic sort: the one wrong slot holds the duplicate, and its index gives the missing number

approaches.name: Count each number with a scan
approaches.idea: For every v from 1 to n, count how many times it appears: twice means repeated, zero means missing.
steps: For `v` from 1 to n, count the elements equal to `v`.
A count of 2 gives the repeated value; a count of 0 gives the missing one.
approaches.why: n values, each counted with a full scan.

approaches.name: Count array
approaches.idea: Count every value in an array of size n + 1 in one pass, then read off the 2 and the 0.
steps: Fill `count[x]++` for every `x`.
For `v` from 1 to n: `count[v] == 2` is the repeated value, `count[v] == 0` the missing one.
approaches.why: Linear and simple, at the cost of an O(n) count array.

approaches.name: Cyclic sort, then find the wrong slot
approaches.idea: Swap every value v into index v − 1. Exactly one index ends up wrong: the value sitting there is the duplicate and the index tells you the missing number.
steps: Cyclic sort: while `i < n`, if `nums[i] != nums[nums[i] − 1]` swap `nums[i]` into its home, otherwise `i++`.
Find the `i` with `nums[i] != i + 1` and return `[nums[i], i + 1]`.
approaches.why: At most n − 1 swaps plus n increments. All present values reach their homes, so the missing number's home is the only slot left with a wrong value, and the only value that could not go home is the spare copy.

approaches.name: Two equations from sums
approaches.idea: Compared with 1..n, the array's sum is off by dup − missing and its sum of squares by dup² − missing² = (dup − missing)(dup + missing). Divide to get dup + missing, then solve.
steps: `diff` = sum of `nums` − n(n + 1)/2 = dup − missing.
`squares` = sum of squares − n(n + 1)(2n + 1)/6 = dup² − missing².
`total = squares / diff` = dup + missing; then dup = (total + diff)/2 and missing = (total − diff)/2.
approaches.why: One pass and the input is left untouched. `diff` is never 0 because the duplicate differs from the missing number. Sums of squares reach about 3·10¹¹ for n = 10⁴, so use 64-bit integers in Java and C++.

code.python:
class Solution:
    def findErrorNums(self, nums: List[int]) -> List[int]:
        n = len(nums)
        diff = sum(nums) - n * (n + 1) // 2
        squares = sum(x * x for x in nums) - n * (n + 1) * (2 * n + 1) // 6
        total = squares // diff
        return [(total + diff) // 2, (total - diff) // 2]

find-missing-and-repeated-values.pattern: The grid is one array of n² values from 1..n²: cyclic sort it in place (or use sums)

approaches.name: Count each value with a full scan
approaches.idea: For every v from 1 to n², count its occurrences in the grid.
steps: For `v` from 1 to n², count the cells equal to `v`.
Count 2 → `a`; count 0 → `b`.
approaches.why: n² values, each needing a scan of n² cells. Fine for n ≤ 50 (about 6 million steps), but it does not scale.

approaches.name: Count array
approaches.idea: Count every value in an array of size n² + 1, then read off the 2 and the 0.
steps: For every cell value `x`, `count[x]++`.
For `v` from 1 to n²: `count[v] == 2` is `a`, `count[v] == 0` is `b`.
approaches.why: Each cell is read once. The count array is as big as the grid.

approaches.name: Cyclic sort the grid in place
approaches.idea: Number the cells 0..n² − 1 row by row (cell k is grid[k / n][k % n]). Then it is Set Mismatch: send value v to cell v − 1, and the one wrong cell holds a while its number gives b.
steps: For cell `k` from 0: let `v` be its value and `home = v − 1`. If cell `home` does not already hold `v`, swap the two cells and stay at `k`; otherwise `k++`.
Find the cell `k` whose value is not `k + 1`: return `[its value, k + 1]`.
approaches.why: At most n² − 1 swaps and n² increments, with no memory beyond a few integers. The index arithmetic `k / n`, `k % n` is the only new idea; the rest is the 1D template.

approaches.name: Two equations from sums
approaches.idea: Against 1..n², the grid's sum is off by a − b and its sum of squares by a² − b² = (a − b)(a + b). Divide to get a + b, then solve for both.
steps: `diff` = (sum of cells) − N(N + 1)/2 with N = n², which equals a − b.
`squares` = (sum of squared cells) − N(N + 1)(2N + 1)/6, which equals a² − b².
`total = squares / diff` = a + b; return `[(total + diff) / 2, (total − diff) / 2]`.
approaches.why: One pass over the grid and nothing is modified. With N up to 2500 the sum of squares is about 5·10⁹, beyond 32-bit range, so use long / long long.

code.python:
class Solution:
    def findMissingAndRepeatedValues(self, grid: List[List[int]]) -> List[int]:
        N = len(grid) ** 2
        values = [x for row in grid for x in row]
        diff = sum(values) - N * (N + 1) // 2
        squares = sum(x * x for x in values) - N * (N + 1) * (2 * N + 1) // 6
        total = squares // diff
        return [(total + diff) // 2, (total - diff) // 2]

find-all-duplicates-in-an-array.pattern: Cyclic sort (or sign marking): a value whose home is already taken is a duplicate

approaches.name: Count each value with a scan
approaches.idea: For every v from 1 to n, count it with a full scan; a count of 2 makes it a duplicate.
steps: For `v` from 1 to n, count the elements equal to `v`.
If the count is 2, add `v` to the answer.
approaches.why: n values times a full scan each.

approaches.name: Seen array
approaches.idea: Walk once with a boolean array; a value already marked is a duplicate.
steps: Create `seen` of size n + 1, all false.
For each `x`: if `seen[x]` is already true, add `x` to the answer; otherwise set it.
approaches.why: One pass, but the seen array breaks the constant-space requirement.

approaches.name: Cyclic sort, then read the spare copies
approaches.idea: Swap every value v into index v − 1. A copy whose home is already taken stays put, so after placement every slot i that does not hold i + 1 holds a duplicate.
steps: Cyclic sort: while `i < n`, if `nums[i] != nums[nums[i] − 1]` swap it home, else `i++`.
For every `i` with `nums[i] != i + 1`, add `nums[i]`.
approaches.why: At most n − 1 swaps plus n increments, and only the output list grows. Because each value appears at most twice, each duplicate has exactly one spare copy, so it is reported exactly once.

approaches.name: Sign marking
approaches.idea: For each value v, look at slot |v| − 1. If it is already negative, |v| was seen before; otherwise negate it to record the first sighting.
steps: For each `v` in `nums`, take `home = |v| − 1` (the value may already have been negated).
If `nums[home] < 0`, this is the second sighting: add `home + 1`. Otherwise negate `nums[home]`.
approaches.why: A single pass. The sign is a free bit per slot because every value is positive. Duplicates come out in the order their second copy appears.

array-nesting.pattern: Cycles of a permutation: walk each cycle once (mark visited)

approaches.name: Walk the cycle from every start
approaches.idea: Each set s[k] is the cycle through k. From every index, follow the arrows until you come back to it, counting steps.
steps: For each `start`: set `len = 1` and `i = nums[start]`; while `i != start`, move `i = nums[i]` and `len++`.
Return the largest `len`.
approaches.why: In a permutation the walk always returns to its start, but if the whole array is one cycle, every one of the n starts walks all n steps.

approaches.name: Visited array: each cycle once
approaches.idea: Every index on a cycle gives the same set, so once a cycle has been walked, skip all its indexes.
steps: Keep `seen`. For each `start` not yet seen, walk `i = nums[i]` marking `seen[i]` and counting, until you reach a seen index.
Return the longest walk.
approaches.why: Each index is marked once and never walked again, so all walks together take n steps.

approaches.name: Mark visited in place
approaches.idea: Values are 0..n − 1, so overwrite a visited slot with −1 instead of keeping a separate array.
steps: For each `start`: walk while `nums[i] >= 0`, saving `next = nums[i]`, setting `nums[i] = −1`, moving to `next` and counting.
Return the longest walk.
approaches.why: The same single walk per cycle, with the array doubling as the visited marks. Save `next` before overwriting the slot.

minimum-number-of-operations-to-sort-a-b.pattern: BFS by level, then minimum swaps to sort each level = size − cycles (cyclic sort to sorted positions)

approaches.name: BFS, then selection sort each level counting swaps
approaches.idea: Collect each level with a BFS and selection-sort it, counting the swaps that actually move something. Selection sort happens to use the minimum number of swaps.
steps: BFS level by level, copying each level's values into an array.
For each position `i`, find the smallest value in `a[i..]`; if it is not already at `i`, swap it in and count one operation.
Add up the counts over all levels.
approaches.why: Each swap puts the right value at position i for good, which detaches exactly one element from its cycle: that is all an optimal swap can do, so the count is minimal. But a level can hold about n/2 nodes, and selection sort is quadratic in the level size.

approaches.name: BFS, then cyclic sort each level to its sorted positions
approaches.idea: A value's target is its index in a sorted copy of the level. Cyclic-sort each value to its target, counting swaps: that count is size − cycles, the minimum.
steps: BFS level by level, copying each level's values into `a`.
Sort a copy and map each value to its index in it (its target).
For each `i`: while `a[i]` is not at its target, swap it there and count one operation.
approaches.why: Each swap sends one value to its final position, so a level of size w needs at most w − 1 swaps, which equals w − cycles. Sorting each level dominates: O(w log w) summed over levels is O(n log n). The queue and the map hold one level at a time.

couples-holding-hands.pattern: Greedy seat-pair swaps; the answer is seat pairs − cycles (partner of x is x ^ 1)

approaches.name: Greedy, scanning for the partner
approaches.idea: Fix the seat pairs left to right: if seat 2j + 1 does not hold the partner of the person in seat 2j, find the partner further right and swap them in.
steps: For `i = 0, 2, 4, …`: the partner is `row[i] ^ 1`.
If `row[i + 1]` is not the partner, scan `j > i + 1` for it, swap `row[i + 1]` and `row[j]`, and count one swap.
approaches.why: n seat pairs, each possibly scanning the row. Each swap seats one couple for good and never breaks another, which is why the greedy is optimal (see the last approach). With at most 60 seats this is already fast.

approaches.name: Greedy with a seat index
approaches.idea: The same greedy, but keep seat[person] so the partner is found in O(1). Update both people's seats on every swap.
steps: Build `seat[row[i]] = i`.
For `i = 0, 2, 4, …`: if `row[i + 1]` is not `row[i] ^ 1`, let `j = seat[partner]`; swap `row[i + 1]` and `row[j]`, update their seats, count one swap.
approaches.why: One pass with O(1) work per seat pair. Forgetting to update `seat` for the person moved out of seat i + 1 is the usual bug.

approaches.name: Count cycles with union-find
approaches.idea: Make each couple a node, and join the two couples sitting on each seat pair. A group of k couples tangled together needs k − 1 swaps, so the answer is couples − groups.
steps: Start with n / 2 separate couples (couple of person x is x / 2).
For each seat pair (`2j`, `2j + 1`), union the couples of its two occupants; count every union that merges two groups.
That count, couples − groups, is the answer.
approaches.why: Each couple touches at most two seat pairs, so every group is a cycle (a seated couple is a cycle of one). The goal is one cycle per couple, and a swap can split at most one cycle into two, so at least couples − groups swaps are needed; the greedy reaches it. The number of successful unions is exactly couples − groups.
